reason: R1 is just one of the two load resistors; if you only care about a single-ended output (e.g., VOUT1), you can remove the VOUT2 branch and still have a functioning common-source gain stage on the remaining side. Caveat: you lose true differential operation and symmetry, and VOUT2 will no longer be a valid output node.
impact_estimate: Low impact if single-ended use is acceptable; high impact if differential behavior is required.

reason: M1 is the transistor for the second half of the differential pair; removing it still leaves M0 operating as a basic NMOS amplifier (with its load resistor) provided the bias node IB1 is driven appropriately. Caveat: input VIN2 and the differential-pair behavior (CMRR, differential gain) are lost, and IB1 bias/current distribution assumptions change.
impact_estimate: Low impact for a single-ended amplifier; high impact for a differential amplifier.

reason: If you instead choose to keep the VOUT2 side, you can remove R0 as the redundant load on the other output; the circuit can still function as a single-ended amplifier using VOUT2 (with R1 and M1). Caveat: same as above—removing one load resistor eliminates that output’s DC path and it will not produce a meaningful output.
impact_estimate: Low impact if only one output is needed; high impact if both outputs/differential output are needed.
